How to read a colour decision

Source → profile/space → display/export → viewer. Ask what each step forecloses.

A palette you can defend is a chain of choices you can still see.

(Tao of the Image)

Image: Four concentric squares in orange, light orange, mustard yellow and dark brown, nested so each colour changes how the next is read.

Grafik nach Josef Albers1 · Anonymous graphic after Josef Albers (CC0 upload) · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Model the reading on this slide: How to read a colour decision.
  • Script: Source → profile/space → display/export → viewer. Ask what each step forecloses.
  • Ask one student to restate the path the picture travels.

1 · Colour is a relation

Teach palettes through interaction, contrast, and context — not isolated RGB sliders.

Colour answers to its neighbours before it answers to a number.

(Tao of the Image)

2 · A bitmap has limits

A bitmap is a fixed grid of colour values — mode, depth, and gamut close later options.

Every bit you spend on colour is a door you may not reopen later.

(Tao of the Image)

3 · Platform tones are historical

Creator tools circulate lighting, colour trends, and tones that look “professional” for a season — treat them as signals to compare, not defaults to copy.

Sharing expertise and using specific technologies result in visuality that reflect certain editing styles that are popular at a given moment.

(Roivainen 2025, 8)

4 · The display participates

The same palette on two screens can be two designs — name the display assumption you export under.

The screen is not a mirror; it is a second author of the colour.

(Tao of the Image)

5 · Critical · Who is the default viewer?

When a palette is called accurate or fashionable, ask whose body, display, and cultural code count as neutral — generative tools are not representationally neutral.

This analysis reveals significant racial homogenization, e.g., depicting nearly all Middle Eastern men as bearded, brown-skinned, and wearing traditional attire.

(AlDahoul et al. 2025)

6 · Correcting vs changing

When does “correcting” a colour become “changing” the garment it depicts? Decide together — then keep the decision visible.

Correction without disclosure is a redesign with an alibi.

(Tao of the Image)

Exercise 1 · Lock the key-visual brief, then sample a palette

Write audience, channel, and one claim before opening the canvas. Sample five colours from a rights-clear garment photo — then build one accessible alternate.

Name the viewer before you name the hex.

(Tao of the Image)

Brief text + five-colour strip + accessible alternate + one hierarchy note.

Image: Costumes civils HISTORICAL CLOTHING OF FRANCE civilian costumes male female dress fashion design c 1640-1925 Public domain French illustration Larousse du XXème siècle 1932.jpg

Costumes civils HISTORICAL CLOTHING OF FRANCE civilian costumes male female dress fashion design c 1640-1925 Public domain French illustration Larousse du XXème siècle 1932 · 19th-century French costume plate engraver · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Timer: 20 minutes. Pairs OK for brief critique; craft is individual. ACT2 key-visual practice.
  • Write audience, channel, and single claim before opening the canvas.
  • Sample five colours from a garment/fabric photo you own or that is rights-clear; build a palette strip.
  • Build one accessible alternate (contrast-aware) without inventing a second claim.
  • Reject any swatch that does not serve the claim.

Source: Classroom adaptation (key-visual / palette craft gap — no Wave-1 verified pedagogy sequence).

Ask: Which colour would you drop first if the channel shrank to a phone crop?

Digital Creativity I · I.3 Colour, bitmap images

Exercise 2 · One Gestalt pass on a key-visual crop

Name one Gestalt relation. Apply it once to a key-visual crop; break it in a second version; keep both.

These styles can emphasise lighting, colour trends, and tones that make images look 'professional' or 'unique'.

(Roivainen 2025, 8)

Two crops (relation / broken relation) + peer one-sentence vote + process note naming the relation.

Image: A historical beauty advertisement

Dorothy Lamour - Woodbury Complete Beauty Cream, 1945 · Woodbury / advertiser (1945 publication) · Rights under review · Source

  • Timer: 20 minutes. Pairs for the peer vote. ACT2 composition craft.
  • Name one Gestalt relation (proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, or figure–ground).
  • Apply it once to a key-visual or fashion crop; invert or break it in a second version.
  • Peer names which version groups more clearly and why (one sentence).
  • Record the chosen relation in the process note.

Source: Classroom adaptation (Gestalt pedagogy gap — Arnheim not in Wave-1 references).

Ask: Did the display (zoom, crop, phone) change which version won?
